title: Book 12 opens: priesthood continued; Levi chosen yet screened for blemish
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK TWELVE. Concerning priesthood.

So then concerning the sacred stole, and indeed also the sacrifices which God was legislating must also be finished upon the perfectings of the priests, it has been said clearly. And with myriad things as many as have been oracled upon them, both concerning liturgy and cleansings, and accurate diligence of the needing to live most lawfully and polished unto intelligible elegance, I at least think it needful also before the others to say that.
Palladius: What sort of thing do you say?

Cyril: For a dedication to God and chosen out from all the tribes was the one from blood of Levi, and law was giving to the race the needing to priest, God apportioning to it the select prize upon this; yet he was not leaving the sacred-working multitude wholly unexamined, nor was he simply releasing the matter to whoever happened, through at least being from blood of Levi; but he was ordering to investigate carefully and very finely, lest somehow some of the blamed things having happened to be sick be unwilled by God, and make the approach blemished, and only not also, rushing in with unwashed feet into the tent of the witness, he should collide and not willingly. And it has been written thus again in Leviticus: ‘And the Lord spoke toward Moses saying: Speak to Aaron: A human from your race into your generations, to whomsoever there should be in him a blemish, will not come forward to offer the gifts of his God. Every human in whom there should be a blemish will not come forward, a human blind, or lame, or flat-nosed, or ear-cut, or a human in whom there is in’
translator_notes: Ends mid ἐν into §2 αὐτῷ σύντριμμα; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Lev 21 list finished; bodily illness not guilt; spiritual type; bishop blameless
english: Cyril: …him a crushing of hand or crushing of foot, or humpbacked, or white-spotted, or thin-lidded the eyes, or a human in whom if there should be in him wild itch, or lichen, or single-testicled; everyone who is in him a blemish from the seed of Aaron the priest will not draw near of the bringing the sacrifices to the Lord, because a blemish is in him. The gifts of his God he will not come forward to bring; the gifts of his God, the Holy of holies, and from the holy things he will eat, yet toward the veil he will not come forward, and toward the altar he will not draw near, because he has a blemish; and he will not profane the holy of his God, because I am Lord the one sanctifying them.’
Palladius: So then, tell me, is bodily sickness unto a charge for some? And does the Creator write nature even unwillingly corrupted?

Cyril: Well done, O Palladius; for you think rightly. For cause and writing would sometimes become for some who have voluntary the turning-aside of their own mind unto the base things, and who have prized the inclination unto anything whatsoever of the outlandish; but to blame for the sicknesses around the flesh, happening naturally and unwillingly, I somehow think hard and unsympathetic, and not without share of the charges unto left-handedness. So then it is possible from here to think around that, that the creator of the wholes would not have written the nature of a human upon unwilling causes, nor would he as unholy have sent out the one sick bodily from the liturgy arranged with him; but as again from type of the bodily things he thins us down unto more elegant counsels, and under-shows the many-formed of the passions in soul, and gives to think that the matter is God-hated. Or did not also all-divine Paul say that the well-famed vote upon all the marvelled-at things must follow those chosen unto priesthood? ‘In order that,’ he says, ‘the human of God may be complete, fully fitted unto every good work.’ And indeed he insisted that the bishop also must be unreprovable, and very clearly; and in these he was making much accuracy.
Palladius: I say so. And what then would be also the word upon each of the sicknesses just now numbered for us, I would wish, as you well know, to learn.

Cyril: Come then part by part, taking up as in a form, let us say the things going into mind: ‘A human,’ he says, ‘into your generations, from your race, in whom if there should be in him a blemish, will not come forward to offer the gifts of his God.’ Safe the word, bitter the oracle. For the law has been set not against only those then come from Aaron, but it extends unto all the race, and against every priestly blood, and creeps through unto every time. For this, I think, makes clear the, ‘From your race into your generations.’ For always somehow unacceptable to God is what does not have blamelessly. And a time one would not be able to say, according to which the condemned would become dear to him, as rather upon the spiritual sicknesses;
translator_notes: Ends mid πνευματικαῖς· into §3 ἐκτετίμηται; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Blameless prized in Christ-priest race; blind = mindless; lame = weak zeal
english: Cyril: …and rather the having blamelessly has been prized, and sick nowhere the corruption, complete as it were unto virtue, and well-strong unto sanctification, the having practiced well to be well-reputed in endurance, and keen unto continual understanding. Therefore also going against all the race he makes the law upon this, showing forth for himself the sacred and chosen race unadulterated; then as in tribe Levi, and as from blood of Aaron, but now at least as in those sanctified in Christ the great and according to truth high priest, to whom we have grown attached through spirit, shown forth partners and sharers of his own nature. Therefore also having called unto brotherhood those justified in faith, as with partners he rejoices saying: ‘Behold I and the children whom God gave me.’ Or did it not seem to all-divine Paul also to attach the word upon this to the person of Christ?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: So then he bars from the needing to priest the one upon whichever of the named, as sick and mocked. For he will not come forward, he says, to offer the gifts of God, a human blind or lame. So then the matter has from itself, even if thought bodily, much the unbeautiful; for with eyes having flowed out, and indeed also a foot not firmly set, not having to walk straight, how is it not better to be still, neither knowing where at all the priest must go, or else to go with laughter, using another’s foot and eyes? But the word of this would not be much. But the necessary unto knowledge and spiritual contemplation for us, come let us say, running under the thick of the history. So then blind he seems to call the very simple and mindless. For what eye is to the earthy body, this also in soul would be said the mind, lit up by the divine light, and opening toward the pure beauty itself, and by the thin as it were and well-turning motions of thoughts leaping up very well toward the accurate in glory, and knowing not to miss dogmatic rightness. This, I think, is the proverbially said, ‘Let your eyes look straight things, and let your eyelids nod just things.’ And it has been said somewhere also toward the mother of the Jews looking not rightly: ‘Behold your eyes are not, nor is your heart good, but unto your greed and unto pouring out the innocent blood itself, and unto your injustices, and unto murder of doing them.’ So then unsuitable unto sacred-work is the blind intelligibly, that is the wholly ununderstanding, and damaged in mind and sense. And unsuitable besides this also the lame, that is a man not knowing to walk-straight, and not well-strong unto walking completely. For blindness, just as I said just now, is a symbol of extreme ununderstanding; but lameness again, of the as it were broken and weak motion and eagerness which one might make upon each of the things to be done. Unless it is worthy to cry upon those thus damaged:
notes_covered: Heb 2:13 children; Christ high priest race
translator_notes: Ends mid ἐπιφωνεῖν ἄξιον· into §4 Isaiah quote; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Strengthen weak hands; flat-nose = poor discernment; cut-ear = hard-hearing; crush of foot/hand
english: Cyril: ‘Be strong, hands slackened, and knees paralyzed.’ And Christ himself also was blaming the peoples of the Jews, as not enduring to make the tracks upon him straight, but rather turned out unto the lame, and slipped from the reasonings of rightness. ‘For alien sons,’ he says, ‘lied to me; alien sons grew old, and they limped from their paths.’ So then in equal to one another and very near, as in likeness of passions, are lameness of mind and blindness; the one bringing down unto uselessness the precious as in understanding, the other the well-strong as in good works. And besides these the law said the flat-nosed must be made rejectable, and with him the ear-cut. And one might fit upon them such a word. For by the smelling senses both the foul-smelling and most fragrant are tested, of as many as are in such a nature, the one allotted to smell, I mean; and very discerning is the sense, both of what knows how to delight, and of what not somehow thus, but having otherwise, and as in a worse share; and human mind at least, if it should somehow have completely in the things according to itself, goes well-strongly unto being able to discern the quality of the things, and will make the accurate assay upon each, and like some excellent banker testing all things, and holding the good, and abstaining from every form of evil, according to what has been written, will be well-reputed very much. For it adulterates the as it were shameful and counterfeit of the things done, and would easily accept the beneficial and better. So then snub-nosedness makes clear the not very healthy and completely having as in sense, according to which discerning each of the things best, apportioning the better vote to the best, and the worse to the more shameful, we both are and have been named wise and keen-minded, and what not of such things. For smell as it were leaping up into mind is as it were a real quality of the things thought by it. And the having been cut-off of the ear would under-show, as at least it seems to me, the hard-hearing. For with hearing cut-off, I at least would grant the passion to be the from-part obedient, and not wholly well-reined unto obedience, or else the not being able blamelessly to hear the sacred, especially writings, which indeed some also do, most counsel-lessly turning aside the well-hearing of the soul unto things not fitting. And these would be, according to the voice of all-wise Paul, those itching the hearing, and turning it away from the truth, and lying upon spirits of error, and having inclined unto profane empty-voices. So then the ear-cut would under-show the maiming of the inward and intelligible hearing, and the corruption from rightness unto the worse. But also if somehow a crushing of foot or crushing of hand should be seen present for someone, let him withdraw, he says, and be ranked in equal with the others, this persuading to think the one somehow crushed in foot or hand, yet not altogether sick,
translator_notes: Ends mid ἠῤῥωστηκότος, into §5 τὸν οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Partial crush = careless work; humpbacked = earth-bent; white-spot = shameless open vice
english: Cyril: …the one not wholly able to go unto works, nor indeed having the walking wholly unreproachable, or the energy, the as in citizenship, I mean, and most lawful life. And these again would be either those doing the work of the Lord carelessly, upon whom the woe has been brought through a prophet’s voice, or those pursuing the just not justly, according to what has been written. And observe that to the intelligible and whole lameness, also the moderate maiming of the leg is in equal, and has been reckoned as the same. For to being able to do nothing at all of the good things, the not doing rightly will lie in equal word. And reasonably it would appear in the lameness the not-at-all; and in the crushing the not-healthily.
Palladius: It seems so.

Cyril: And humpbacked, and white-spotted, and thin-lidded the eyes he writes down again as among the most unapproved. And humpbacked we say to be the as it were bent-over, and looking down with mind, and inclined toward the passions of flesh, and fixing the eye upon the earthly things—clear that the intelligible—and going unto this of judgment thereafter, so as to hate being set upright, toward at least the needing to think the things above. And in these would be the charges of the Jews, about whom it has been written: ‘Let their eyes be darkened of the not seeing, and bend together their back through all.’ And white-spotted, the one having the so-called white-spot upon their foreheads. And this sickness blackens in form the look upon the tip of skin. And it takes away from those for whom it should happen to suffer, the even at least being able to escape notice, flowering upon the brows themselves, and hung upon whole faces. So then such a one white-spotted bodily, but intelligibly under-shows the unseemly, nakedly and unhiddenly, and as it were not having a clean face, but the unbeautiful unto life manifest to all, so as perhaps not even to know somewhere the rightly said by one of the wise, ‘Wise will hide their own shames.’
Palladius: How did you say?
Cyril: For are there not, O Palladius, myriad as many passions in us?
Palladius: Yes; what then is this?

Cyril: That, O noble one, I say, each is sick what he is sick, but often being worsted by shame toward brothers, he makes in zeal and much word both seeming to be healthy, and escaping notice in evils.
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: But if somehow someone should have come unto such shamelessness as to think as nothing also choosing to sin openly, and to spare completely the prizes unto seemliness, would such a one thereafter not seem to someone to have gone far from the sacred and holy race?
Palladius: And very much.
Cyril: So then the law calls such a one white-spotted, as not even knowing and enduring to hide the sickness and passion that happened to him. And thin-lidded the
notes_covered: crush = careless Lord’s work / unjust justice
translator_notes: Ends mid Πτιλὸν δὲ τοὺς into §6 ὀφθαλμοὺς; PG mid-cut kept. Sirach allusion tentative.

title: Thin-lidded eyes = see yet not rightly; wild itch / lichen / extreme passion
english: Cyril: …eyes, the one least deprived of seeing, yet not having to do this healthily. Of which sort some would be, for whom understanding is present, yet the choosing to think rightly is not seen present. For some seeing, he says, the good, turn aside the inclination of their own wills unto things not fitting; and others, even being able not to be without share of dogmatic rightness, only not themselves damage their own mind, going unto a most unbeautiful hunt of thoughts, and receiving nothing healthy of the glory upon God; of which sort are especially children of heretics, and Jews besides, who believe the Father to be God, yet most mindlessly thrust away the Son who has appeared from him according to nature. Therefore also true upon them is the hymned through a prophet’s voice, ‘Eyes for them, and they do not see.’ For seeing benefits nothing, unless somehow the seeing healthily should be foreseen for some, just as indeed we were saying justly that both lameness and the crushing of the foot have been ranked in equal word; for it will differ wholly nothing, from not being able to go at all, the somehow not going healthily, clearly the path as in affairs, and the road as in works.
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: And a human will not come forward about to sacred-work, in whom if there should be upon him wild itch, or lichen, or single-testicled, or everyone in whom there is a blemish. So then to wild itch must be likened the most outlandish of the passions, poured down upon mind with sharper flows, and going beyond every measure, and having beginning from pleasure, yet finishing unto a bitter end. Or do you not say that for each of the miss-doings both some measure and unmeasure of the evil is seen?
Palladius: How did you say?

Cyril: The one worsted by bodily pleasure—would he not suffer this both moderately and beyond measure? For some are only worsted, and are sick restrainedly; and others also come unto the tip of the evil, and are sick the pleasure raging uncontrollably, so as even to slip beyond the passions according to nature themselves.
Palladius: I understand what you say.

Cyril: So then upon each of the evils the having inclined outlandishly unto beyond word, and beyond measures of the in custom and among many, would thereafter be said the wild itch. And lichen besides, any passion whatsoever, always creeping unto the broad, and having unceasing the increase unto the worse. And the divine law wills that the falling passions must be contracted by us, and led unto the lesser. You will think some such thing hearing: ‘If spirit of the one exercising authority should rise upon you, do not leave your place, because a healing will stop great sins.’ For the unreproved of the passions always creep toward the more shamefully having; and they seize heart and mind, and lead unto complete destruction. So then the base must be blamed by us, with the runnings-up unto the better wrapping
notes_covered: thin lids = see without healthy sight; heretics/Jews
translator_notes: Ends mid περιστελ into §7 λούσης; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Single-testicled = half-man / soft; may eat holy yet barred from altar; shared weakness warned
english: Cyril: …it of the sobriety in us, and destroying little by little. And single-testicled besides, he says, just as I at least think, the half-man, and as it were cut-off the perfectly manly. ‘For neither fornicators,’ he says, ‘nor soft ones will inherit the kingdom of God.’ And he names such ones womanish, because having obtained a man’s nature they lie about the manly, soft in both mind and body, and willingly bent toward the unmanly and woman-fitting. And it is likely again that the single-testicled also under-shows something else. For it is custom to name a man the well-strong and compacted, and not insufficiently having unto being able to set upright whatever he might somehow choose. And reasonably half a man would be thought the not wholly well-strong, nor altogether keen unto the things fitting him; for it is not fitting for the one lying upon God to bring forward courage cut-apart for him and the well-strong damaged, and as to be weak from part; but to play-the-man and be strong, according to what has been written, having unreproachable and unmocked eagerness. So then unholy admittedly is the one under a writing of blemish. Yet he is not barred from the needing to share the holy food. ‘For he will eat from the holy things,’ he says, ‘yet toward the veil he will not come forward, and toward the altar he will not draw near.’ For those still liable to the inward hidden weaknesses unto mind would share the blessing of Christ, and not as in the rank of the saints unto increase of sanctification, and unto firmness of mind, and the remaining firmly set upon all the best things, but as in the manner fitting those sick unto putting away of the evil, and unto cessation of sin, and unto deadening of pleasures, and unto taking-up of spiritual good-condition. For since Christ is a new creation, according to the Scriptures, in this way we also receive him in ourselves through his holy flesh and blood, in order that being re-elemented unto newness of life through him and in him, we may put off the old human, the one being corrupted according to the desires of deceit, according to what has been written.
Palladius: You spoke rightly.

Cyril: So then he denies the practice of the sacred works to those somehow having the intelligible outrage melted-in and irremovable sick; for least holy is what is always sick the grown-on of the passions; but if also for someone of those having blamelessly at least in themselves, and unreproachably unto liturgy, the being sick of these common and not fading passions happens, he orders that he must not be left unreproved, saying: ‘Speak toward Aaron and toward his sons, and let them take heed from the holy things of the sons of Israel, and they will not profane my holy name, as many as they themselves sanctify for me; I am Lord. Speak to them: Into your generations every human who should come forward from all the seed’
notes_covered: Christ new creation; put off old human
translator_notes: Ends mid σπέρματος into §8 ὑμῶν πρὸς τὰ ἅγια; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Lev 22 uncleanness; leper and flux barred; types of soul-death and barren mind
english: Cyril: …of you toward the holy things, as many as the sons of Israel should sanctify to the Lord, and his uncleanness should be upon him, that soul will be utterly destroyed from me. I am Lord your God, and a human from the seed of Aaron the priest, and this one is leprous or has a flow of seed, will not eat of the holy things until he should be cleansed, and the one touching every uncleanness of soul, or a human from whom a bed of seed should go out, or whoever should touch every unclean creeping thing which defiles him, or upon a human in whom it defiles him according to every uncleanness of him; a soul which if it should touch them will be unclean until evening, will not eat from the holy things unless he should wash his body with water, and the sun should set, and he will be clean, and then he will eat of the holy things, because it is his bread. He will not eat a carcass and a beast-taken, lest he be defiled in them. I am Lord, and they will keep my keepings, in order that they may not take sin through them, and die through them, if they should profane them. I am Lord the one sanctifying them.’ For those bringing the sacred things, he says, or the things being sanctified by the sons of Israel, as many as they should dedicate unto sacrifice to God, let them not profane his name, bringing not pre-purified, and still having unwashed the uncleanness which it happens to suffer; or let them know that, he says, they will at once pay the last justice. For I am Lord, that is, not a falsely-named god, against whom even if somehow one should sin, nothing will be a miss-deed. For what would even become from us unto wood or stone, to which also the needing to be corrected would follow? So then correcting unto safety of the uncleanness by the very fears, he usefully numbers the manners according to which it would become from us, so that the ministers may know the road of the fairness most fitting them, and through which they would be both acceptable and clean, walking through the life most dear to the lawgiver.
Palladius: You spoke rightly.

Cyril: So then the leprous and the one with flow of seed he both sets out from the sacred liturgy, and says he must become without share of the holy things, until he should thrust away from himself what happened, and become farthest from being sick. And he joins to these, as sick a same-natured uncleanness, the one touching every uncleanness of soul, or for whom if a bed of seed should go out, and indeed the one touching a creeping thing, and of a man having any denunciation upon pollution; not, I think, the law blaming bodily passions, according at least to the true and blamelessly having aim, but as still in types, by the in-sense and bodily things, showing forth the things in souls. So then a symbol of deadness is leprosy; for it consumes and grazes down the flesh, and changes unto the against-nature, and alters the look of the body. And flow of seed is a putting-away of fruit-bearing, nature flowing unto nothing; of which sort also a human mind would be seen carried aside unto corruption and only not being consumed unto barrenness, through at least being able to understand nothing of the neces
translator_notes: Ends mid ἀναγ into §9 καίων εἰς σωτηρίαν; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Hymenaeus/Alexander; unworthy eating; touching uncleanness = shared counsel/deed
english: Cyril: …sary unto salvation; of which sort Hymenaeus and Alexander have become, both thinking and saying resurrection has already happened. And to these would be added those inclining unbridledly toward anything whatsoever of the outlandish, and simply casting aside the fruit of their own mind unto stale and wanton pleasures. So then the leprous and the one with flow of seed, that is, the one held in works of deadness (and works of deadness would be the passions of the flesh), and the one not having the inward fruit-bearing, clearly the unto mind and hidden, uncorrupted, let him withdraw, he says, from the holy things, until he should be cleansed. For as all-divine Paul said, ‘Whoever should eat the body of the Lord and drink his cup unworthily, eats and drinks judgment for himself, not discerning his body. But let a human,’ he says, ‘test himself, and then eat from the bread, and drink from the cup.’
Palladius: You spoke best.

Cyril: So then observe, O Palladius, the accuracy of the law; for it has least gone against only the leprous and the one with flow of seed, but as it were also condemns-with them, even if somehow someone should touch those sick, I mean leprous and with flow of seed. ‘And the one touching,’ he says, ‘every uncleanness of soul, or for whom a bed of his seed should go out, will be unclean.’
Palladius: And what damage from this would become for those touching?

Cyril: None at least, according to the word in ready hand. For touch of body will not defile a human’s soul. But the law is spiritual, and teaches us again riddlingly, that unclean in charges of pollutions are those liable to soul-passions. And those touching are defiled-with them, or clinging, clearly according to relation of same-counsel, or same-deed; ‘For evil companies corrupt good customs’; and, ‘No share for a faithful with an unfaithful’; and enemy and irreconcilable to the dark is the light. And true that ‘With a holy one you will be holy, and with an innocent man you will be innocent, and with a chosen one you will be chosen, and with a crooked one you will twist.’ And that not only being sick the most outlandish of the passions will be all-hard for those sick alone, but also whoever should become same-minded and same-opinioned will be defiled with pollutions not less than those, he showed at once adding, that ‘Whoever if he should touch every unclean creeping thing will defile him, or upon a human in whom he defiles according to every uncleanness of him, a soul which should touch them will be unclean until evening.’ And bitter and venom-shooting creeping things we say both to be said and to be those for whom the word would be fitting, ‘Venom of asps under their lips; whose mouth is full of curse and bitterness.’ And these would be also before the others those twisting the straight things, and sounding into the simpler ones the word that procures destruction, carrying them off toward thoughts not good, and unto glory upon God the
translator_notes: Ends mid τὴν δι into §10 εστραμμένην; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Twisted glory; until evening = before Immmanuel; wash + sunset = baptism / living bread
english: Cyril: …twisted, or also those somehow saying: ‘Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die’; and those dragging out the minds of the more unlearned toward the pleasure-loves in world. And unclean again and knowing how to defile those touching, or going near, according at least, I say, to the law of disposition, are those about whom all-wise Paul also somehow said: ‘If someone named a brother is a fornicator, or a drunkard, or a snatcher, or a greedy one, or an idolater, with such a one not even to eat-together.’ Or do you not say that most fitting for the sacred and chosen race is the needing not to have become such evils, nor indeed to be mixed-together with those sick?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: ‘So then he will be in uncleanness,’ he says, ‘whoever should touch these, until evening. He will not eat from the holy things unless he should wash his body with water, and the sun should set, and he will be clean, and then he will eat from the holy things, because it is his bread.’ And besides these still he denies the eating of a carcass and beast-taken, as able sufficiently to defile. So then see, O Palladius, the putting-away of every filth, and release from charges, not otherwise becoming in us, except through Christ alone, and as in the time of the sojourn.
Palladius: How did you say?

Cyril: That everything before the sojourn of the Only-begotten is uncleaned and still in pollutions, and without share of life, he showed saying: ‘He will be unclean until evening, and will not eat from the holy things.’ Or did Emmanuel not sojourn in the last times of the age?
Palladius: Yes; for clear is the word.

Cyril: And we have been made alive having eaten down the bread, the truly holy and from heaven, that is Christ, the time having come unto an end, and as it were a sun setting, and shutting the measure of time unto evening.
Palladius: Very much.

Cyril: In this way also until evening unclean is the polluted, and without share also of holy and life-making food, waiting the time of the cleansing. And having washed with water and with sun having set, clean, and having as own bread the from heaven. For as it were it has been apportioned to those sanctified through water, as in holy baptism, I mean, the being blessed through Christ; and indeed he himself is the living bread, and he himself again the one having come down from heaven, and giving life to the world. And that the setting of sun would mark the time of our Savior’s sojourn, you will know clearly, with God saying upon the lamb toward the hierophant Moses: ‘Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them take for themselves a sheep according to houses, and it will be, he says, kept from the tenth of the month until the fourteenth, and they will slaughter it, all the’
notes_covered: 1 Cor 5:11 not eat with named brother
translator_notes: Ends mid πᾶν τὸ into next section; PG mid-cut kept.
